prompt: What public tools or databases identify functions in a PowerPC GameCube/Wii DOL/REL by content and map them to known names or sources across games: dtk signatures, Ghidra BSim or Function ID databases, IDA FLIRT/Lumina-style PowerPC signatures, Dolphin symbol maps (.map/.dsy) and signature generators, masked-byte or relocation-aware hashing used to transfer matched functions between decomps? Give repo URLs, licences, how they mask relocations and how they report false matches. For every claim give the primary source (repo file, issue, PR, compiler manual) and state it as a falsifiable prediction: 'with X, mwcc emits Y; with X', it emits Y''. Mark anything unverified.

query: What measured results exist on how often content-based function matching between GameCube and Wii decompilation projects returns the wrong name or the wrong source file, and who reported those mismatches?

When a decompilation project imports function names from another game's finished work by matching compiled code, how often does the imported name turn out to be wrong, and who has counted those errors?

Why do two different functions, or two copies of the same library function, end up with identical or near-identical machine code, and how does that cause a matching tool to assign the wrong name or the wrong source file?

Why do two copies of the same function compiled by the Metrowerks compiler end up with different bytes, and how do relocations, register allocation, inlining and linker-generated stubs change what a matcher sees?

What measured data exists on how often the same C source compiled with different Metrowerks CodeWarrior versions or flag settings produces different PowerPC instructions, and who in decompilation projects has recorded those differences?
Why does the Metrowerks linker sometimes insert branch stubs or veneers or rewrite relocated addresses, and what happens to the bytes a matching tool compares when it does?

What happens to function matching when the same library code was built with a different SDK version, compiler build, or optimization level, and at what point does a signature database stop recognizing it or start naming the wrong function?

Why does a compiler that inlines a small function, or merges and reorders code, leave a binary where a signature built from the standalone library function can no longer find it, and what does the wrong or missing result look like to the analyst?

Which reverse engineering teams or researchers have reported that automatic function matching or signature recognition worked reliably on heavily optimized, inlined or template-generated code, and what did their setup do differently from the cases where it failed?
Are there decompilation projects that skipped signature databases and shared function names across games by other means, and did they get better or worse results than the signature-based approach?

How often do two games from the same studio and console generation, built with different compiler versions or library releases, end up with functions that look identical in the machine code but have different names or different behavior, and what do decompilation teams report about the cleanup work this causes?

Why do automated function-matching tools that compare control-flow structure, constants and call relationships succeed on some binaries and fail on others, and what in the compiled code decides whether a match is reliable?

learning: [DERIVED][LOW] A matching decompilation only proves one specific compiler turns the C into the original bytes, not that the C means the same thing to another compiler or ABI. In the V-Rally port, a set of matched functions each behaved wrongly once built for another target, including cars starting backwards, textures loading at 0 by 0 pixels and sign errors turning 255 into -1. Any name or semantics inferred from a match should be treated as unverified until run under a different build. — Capacidad: You can stop treating a byte-for-byte match as proof that a function's imported name or behavior is correct, and budget separate behavioral checks before trusting matched code. — Evidencia: S6 lists roughly ten specific V-Rally bugs, each in functions that matched byte for byte with KMC GCC 2.7.2, plus Super Mario 64 cases kept under AVOID_UB. — Ledger: C4 (S6)

[DERIVED][LOW] The sources point to cheap behavior checks that surface errors a match hides: building under a second modern compiler, building a port, and comparing memory against the running original. Super Mario 64 already runs a host GCC syntax check alongside the IDO build, and every bug on the V-Rally page was found by building a port. A progress percentage from a match checker is not a correctness measure. — Capacidad: You can decide to fund a second-compiler or port build as a cheap error detector instead of relying on match percentage as the quality measure. — Evidencia: S6 says every bug listed came from building a port and cites SM64's host-compiler check; S4 notes decomp.me scores single functions and never sees other bytes, so scores cannot reveal behavior errors. — Ledger: C5 (S6)

[DERIVED][LOW] None of the supplied sources quantify how often names imported by matching code across games turn out wrong, or name anyone who has counted. The nearest evidence is anecdotal bug lists in one port and the Decomperson study's 300 successful perfect decompilations out of 35,000 submissions, which measures human matching success, not name accuracy. Any decision relying on a rate would rest on an assumption. — Capacidad: You can stop expecting a published error rate for imported function names and plan to measure it yourself, since none of these sources count it. — Evidencia: Across S4, S6, S7, S8 and S9 no figure addresses incorrect imported names; S4 gives only the Decomperson 35,000 submissions and 300 successes. — Ledger: C6 (S4)

[DERIVED][MEDIUM] The mwcc-rs project defines parity as emitting the same relocatable object as the real Metrowerks compiler, byte for byte, and treats an exact .text section alone as useful evidence but not parity. It also keys on section ordering, symbol order, alignment, and relocations such as R_PPC_EMB_SDA21. Comparing at the object stage, before addresses are assigned, avoids layout-dependent changes made at link time. — Capacidad: You can decide to run byte-exact verification on relocatable object files, where the compiler's output is authoritative, instead of on final linked images, which cuts out linker-induced noise. — Evidencia: S18 states the goal is the same relocatable object byte for byte and lists relocation types and section details as part of what must match, with 4,523 commits of work behind that approach. — Ledger: C16 (S18)

[DERIVED][LOW] Behavior of a library function can legitimately differ depending on which SDK version the calling code was built against, and a single program can mix modules built against different SDK versions, including static libraries. A matched function name therefore does not guarantee the same behavior or body as the reference, which raises the risk of a confident but wrong identification. — Capacidad: You can stop trusting a library-name or version match as proof that the same code is inside a binary, and require evidence on the specific function before acting on an identification. — Evidencia: S23 describes SDK-version-dependent behavior and mixed-SDK modules and static libraries in one program; applying that to signature matching is inference. — Ledger: C19 (S23)

[DERIVED][LOW] Shared libraries such as glibc keep multiple versioned implementations of the same function, for example memcpy@GLIBC_2.2.5 alongside memcpy@@GLIBC_2.14, and binaries built years apart bind to different ones. Matching must therefore cover every retained variant, and a database that stores only the newest will miss or mislabel older builds. — Capacidad: You can expect that the same function appears as several coexisting variants within one library, so a database holding only one variant will under-recognize binaries built against older versions. — Evidencia: S24 gives the concrete glibc example of memcpy@GLIBC_2.2.5 and memcpy@@GLIBC_2.14 coexisting, though the signature-database consequence is inferred. — Ledger: C20 (S24)

[DERIVED][LOW] When every call to a function is inlined and its address is never taken, the compiler emits no standalone copy of that function at all, so a signature built from the standalone version has nothing to match. A 'not found' result can therefore mean the code is present but dissolved into its callers, not that the library was never used. — Capacidad: You can stop expecting a standalone library function to appear as a separate, findable routine in a shipped binary, and treat a missing match as a possible sign of inlining rather than proof the library is absent. — Evidencia: GCC documentation states no assembler code is output for an inline static function when all calls are integrated, and the Wikipedia inline-function article says the same for functions that are inlined everywhere. — Ledger: C21 (S25)

[DERIVED][LOW] Inlining puts a separate copy of the function body at each call site, and then optimizes each copy in its caller's context. Constants passed in can fold away branches, so no two copies need look alike or look like the standalone function. A signature may match some copies, none, or fire inconsistently, and an inlined function called 10 times yields 10 differing copies instead of one. — Capacidad: You can expect a library function to match differently from one location to the next in the same binary, and plan analysis around partial or inconsistent hits rather than a single clean match. — Evidencia: Source S25 describes 10 copies of an inlined function and constant propagation, dead code elimination and branch folding after inlining, from which the signature-mismatch consequence is inferred. It does not discuss signatures. — Ledger: C22 (S25)

[DERIVED][LOW] Inlining is largely an optimizing-build behavior: GCC inlines nothing without optimization unless forced, so debug-style builds keep standalone functions that signatures can find, while optimized release builds may erase them. Compilers also differ in what they can inline, so results vary across toolchains. — Capacidad: You can judge how much to trust a 'library absent' or 'library present' finding by asking about build settings, since the same source can yield very different binaries depending on optimization level and compiler. — Evidencia: GCC's manual says no function is really inline without -O, and the Wikipedia C/C++ inline article says compilers vary in how complex a function they can inline and that inlining typically requires optimization to be enabled. — Ledger: C23 (S27)

[DERIVED][LOW] None of the contents describe a project that shared function names across games through a shared-name database or comparable mechanism; the real trade-off documented is between matching decompilation (years per game, human-readable, byte-exact proof of equivalence) and static recompilation (weeks to months, unreadable machine-translated C, but a fast native port). Recompilation gives speed but not understanding, so teams return to a decompilation when behavior must be changed. — Capacidad: You can pick between three reverse-engineering routes for a legacy game or binary (readable byte-exact rebuild, readable behavior-equivalent rebuild, or machine-translated port) based on whether you need proof of correctness, moddability, or speed. — Evidencia: S9 gives a comparison table with time per game (weeks to months for static recompilation vs years for matching decompilation) and describes N64Recomp, released May 2024, translating MIPS straight into C. — Ledger: C24 (S9)

[DERIVED][LOW] Signature databases only auto-name statically linked standard libraries such as zlib, Lua, or the C runtime. Game-specific naming came from strings, imports, and accidental debug leftovers: Devilution used a symbols file left on the Japanese PlayStation disc plus a debug build hidden in the PC data archives, and Silent Hill's team had to reverse-engineer an undocumented internal Konami vibration library by hand. Signature fingerprinting therefore does not reach proprietary engine code. — Capacidad: You can stop assuming that signature databases are the main way decompilers name functions, and plan for the human-labor and leftover-debug-artifact routes that actually carry most projects. — Evidencia: S9 limits signature databases to known libraries and credits leftovers for Devilution; S30 shows an undocumented internal library needing manual reverse engineering. Neither compares result quality against a no-signature approach, so the conclusion is inferred. — Ledger: C25 (S9, S30)

[DERIVED][LOW] The AI-assisted Silent Hill port relied on generative models to guess missing logic and produced frequent crashes and inconsistent flashlight behavior, while the 45-contributor human team spent over two years reaching a readable, accurate decompilation. AI has also sharply cut timelines elsewhere, but the community's byte-for-byte compile-and-diff check is what separates proven equivalence from code that merely looks right. — Capacidad: You can treat AI-generated reconstruction as fast but unreliable, and insist on a byte-for-byte check or human review before trusting or investing in a port built that way. — Evidencia: S30 reports the 45-contributor, two-plus-year effort versus the AI port's crashes; S9 notes matching decompilation proves equivalence and that code that merely looks right proves nothing. — Ledger: C26 (S9, S30)
